body:
**What retail cannot borrow:**
- microsecond latency and co-location;
- cross-asset order-flow visibility;
- portfolio-level delta and vega hedging;
- member-level costs;
- the balance sheet to warehouse tail risk or move an index;
- management access, expert networks and alternative data at scale.

**What retail can borrow:**
- **Selling the volatility premium:** Avoid being the systematic buyer of short-dated OTM options, since that is the side that pays the premium. If trading options at all, prefer defined-risk structures, longer tenors and small size. Note that short options carry tail risk that firms hedge and retail usually cannot.
- **Cost discipline:** Lower turnover, because cost is the one certain loss.
- **Position sizing and risk limits:** Pre-defined stop-out and capital-at-risk rules, mimicking prop risk desks.
- **Systematic process:** Rules-based entries over discretionary impulse.
- **Permanent capital:** Retail with no redemptions can hold through drawdowns that force institutions to sell. Forced FPI index-weight selling, as in 2025–26, can create entry points in quality names.

**Where retail has a structural edge:**
- **Small and micro caps:** These are too small for large funds and FPIs to build meaningful positions.
- **Long horizons:** Retail has no quarterly performance or career risk.
- **No benchmark hugging:** Retail can hold concentrated positions.
- **Ignoring flow-driven selling:** Retail can disregard allocation-driven selling unrelated to fundamentals.

These edges apply to investing, not to short-term F&O.

`person:ed-thorp` | confidence: **verified** | tags: us, process, quant, position-sizing, base-rate

Mathematician who proved blackjack card counting (Beat the Dealer, 1962) and then applied the same logic to markets: only bet when you can quantify a positive expectation, and size by the Kelly criterion. Princeton Newport Partners (Nov 1969-1988): ~19.1% gross / ~15.1% net annualised (some sources say 20% net), with one source reporting 227 winning months and 3 losing months (all <1%). Structural edge: early mathematical pricing of warrants and options (a Black-Scholes-like formula before 1973), convertible arbitrage, statistical arbitrage - hedged, market-neutral books. The fund closed after the 1988 RICO raid tied to the Drexel investigation; Thorp was never charged. He also spotted Madoff in 1991 by noticing the options volume Madoff claimed to trade did not exist. Mistake: the partnership's structural dependence on a partner's office (the RICO case) ended a great record - operational/counterparty risk, not market risk. Copyable for individuals: (1) half-Kelly or smaller sizing - never bet so big that a loss ends the game; (2) check feasibility of any too-smooth record before trusting it; (3) Thorp himself recommends index funds for most people. Not copyable: arbitrage infrastructure.

| key | value |
|---|---|
| edge_structural | option/convert pricing models, hedged arbitrage |
| edge_process | positive expectation + Kelly sizing |
| track_record | ~19.1% gross, ~15.1% net 1969-1988; 3 losing months of 230 (single-source) |
| mistakes | operational/legal risk via Princeton office |
| copyable | fractional Kelly, fraud feasibility checks, indexing |

Links: strategy:thorp-kelly (about); strategy:position-sizing (illustrates); insight:avoid-ruin (illustrates)

Sources: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_Newport_Partners> ; <https://Www.Wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Thorp> ; <https://moneyweek.com/461698/edward-thorp-the-worlds-greatest-investors> ; <https://www.fool.com/investing/2017/01/26/the-riveting-story-of-edward-thorp.aspx>

`case_study:caplin-point-2009-2026` · tickers: CAPLIPOINT · confidence: verified

Split/bonus-adjusted ₹1.14 (Mar 2009) → ₹733 (Aug 2017) ≈640x; P/E 12.5 → 69 (5.5x) × implied EPS ~117x. Then −68% to ₹238 (Mar 2020) while EPS kept rising (TTM ₹10.6 → ₹23.9): the fall was de-rating, not the business. Second leg: ₹238 → ATH ₹2,835 (Sep 2026), ₹2,085 on 19 Nov 2026 (P/E ~23), ≈1,830x overall. From the 2017 peak the stock made 2.8x on EPS ~5.5x as P/E halved. Early signal: an unglamorous generic-drug exporter that built its own last-mile distribution (Neoethicals) in Guatemala, Nicaragua and neighbours, supplying ~4,000 pharmacies directly and cutting out intermediaries; LatAm ~76% of revenue. OPM rose from ~24% to 36%, ROCE was 60%+ with zero debt, and the stock traded at P/E 5–10 in 2010–13. Later: injectables plant audits/approvals for larger LatAm markets (Colombia INVIMA). Investors who tolerated a 'micro-cap in Chennai selling to Nicaragua' were early. Lesson: niche geography plus distribution control gives very high ROCE; the one deep drawdown came purely from P/E 69 → 13, not earnings.

Key data: **start_year**: 2009; **end_year**: 2026; **start_price**: 1.14; **end_price**: 2085; **multiple**: ~640x to 2017; ~1,830x to Nov 2026; **pe_start**: 12.5; **pe_end**: 68.9; **eps_multiple_implied**: ~117x (2009-17); **max_drawdown**: -68% (2017-20, de-rating only); **early_signals**: own distribution in LatAm; 60%+ ROCE at P/E 5-10; **ended**: not ended; **lesson**: de-rating drawdowns with rising EPS are buyable

body:
**Formula.** Other income / PBT. Also compute **core PBT = PBT − other income**.

**Thresholds.**

| Other income / PBT | Reading |
|---|---|
| < 15% | Fine |
| 15–30% | Explain it |
| > 30% | Flag, unless the company is a cash-rich holding company being valued as such |
| > 100% | The core business loses money |

Remember that Screener puts **exceptional items** inside "Other Income".

**Worked examples, FY26.**

| Company | Other income | PBT | OI/PBT | Core PBT | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eternal | 1,396 | 615 | **227%** | **−781** | Treasury income on IPO and QIP cash funds the P&L |
| IndiGo | 2,755 | −1,960 | n/m | −4,715 | Interest on cash and forex |
| Hindustan Unilever | 4,923 | 18,219 | **27%** | 13,296 | Includes the Kwality Wall's demerger gain (below) |
| Wipro (FY25, IFRS) | interest ₹2,721 cr | profit ₹13,218 cr | ~21% of PAT | | Large treasury, not a flag at that level but strip it for EV/EBIT |
